before:
name: learned_shader
description: 'A user-trained function in a shader: original, approximation and error; ordinary arithmetic or cooperative
  vectors.'
operations:
- create:
    box: agent_graphics_context
    name: renderer
    frame:
      x: 40.0
      y: 40.0
      w: 300.0
      h: 100.0
    properties:
      code: "import afield.graphics.vulkan.util.Options\n\nprop<Window>(window)\nprop<Renderer>(renderer)\n\nOptions.enableVR = false\nOptions.enableHDR = false\nOptions.profiling = false\n\nonce.renderer {\n    window = Window(\"Field\")\n    Renderer(window)\n}\n\nprintln(\"agent graphics renderer ready\")\nstart(renderer::run)\n"
- launch:
    box: agent_graphics_context
    property: code
    type: code
    strand: renderer
    code: "import afield.graphics.vulkan.util.Options\n\nprop<Window>(window)\nprop<Renderer>(renderer)\n\nOptions.enableVR = false\nOptions.enableHDR = false\nOptions.profiling = false\n\nonce.renderer {\n    window = Window(\"Field\")\n    Renderer(window)\n}\n\nprintln(\"agent graphics renderer ready\")\nstart(renderer::run)\n"
- wait:
    frames: 3
- create:
    box: learned_shader
    name: learned shader
    frame:
      x: 400.0
      y: 160.0
      w: 420.0
      h: 100.0
    properties:
      code: |-
        import afield.graphics.shader.learning.*

        prop<LearnedShader>(lab)
        fromContextWithNameOrNull<LearnedShader>("lab")?.close()
        var cooperative = renderer.device.supportsCooperativeVector
        var active = cooperative
        var requestedView = 2
        var animate = true
        var reload = false
        lab = LearnedShader(renderer, cooperative = cooperative)
        controlGroup("learned shader") {
            checkbox("Cooperative vectors", initialValue = cooperative) { cooperative = it }
            slider("0: Original · 1: Learned · 2: Compare", min = 0.0, max = 2.0, step = 1.0, initialValue = 2.0) {
                requestedView = it.toInt()
            }
            checkbox("Animate time", initialValue = true) { animate = it }
            button("Reload trained weights") { if (it) reload = true }
        }
        displayOpen("learned shader")
        println("Compare: original / learned / absolute RGB error × 8. Weights describe a 16 → 32 → 32 → 3 network.")
        frames {
            var time = 0.0
            while (true) {
                if (cooperative != active || reload) {
                    runCatching {
                        val next = LearnedShader(renderer, cooperative = cooperative, attach = false)
                        lab.close()
                        lab = next.attach()
                        active = cooperative
                    }
                        .onFailure {
                            println("Keeping working shader: ${it.message}")
                            cooperative = active
                        }
                    reload = false
                }
                lab.view = requestedView
                if (animate) time += .01
                lab.time = kotlin.math.sin(time).toFloat()
                frame()
            }
        }
            .end { lab.close() }
- connect:
    parent: agent_graphics_context
    child: learned_shader
- launch:
    box: learned_shader
    property: code
    type: code
    strand: scene
    code: |-
      import afield.graphics.shader.learning.*

      prop<LearnedShader>(lab)
      fromContextWithNameOrNull<LearnedShader>("lab")?.close()
      var cooperative = renderer.device.supportsCooperativeVector
      var active = cooperative
      var requestedView = 2
      var animate = true
      var reload = false
      lab = LearnedShader(renderer, cooperative = cooperative)
      controlGroup("learned shader") {
          checkbox("Cooperative vectors", initialValue = cooperative) { cooperative = it }
          slider("0: Original · 1: Learned · 2: Compare", min = 0.0, max = 2.0, step = 1.0, initialValue = 2.0) {
              requestedView = it.toInt()
          }
          checkbox("Animate time", initialValue = true) { animate = it }
          button("Reload trained weights") { if (it) reload = true }
      }
      displayOpen("learned shader")
      println("Compare: original / learned / absolute RGB error × 8. Weights describe a 16 → 32 → 32 → 3 network.")
      frames {
          var time = 0.0
          while (true) {
              if (cooperative != active || reload) {
                  runCatching {
                      val next = LearnedShader(renderer, cooperative = cooperative, attach = false)
                      lab.close()
                      lab = next.attach()
                      active = cooperative
                  }
                      .onFailure {
                          println("Keeping working shader: ${it.message}")
                          cooperative = active
                      }
                  reload = false
              }
              lab.view = requestedView
              if (animate) time += .01
              lab.time = kotlin.math.sin(time).toFloat()
              frame()
          }
      }
          .end { lab.close() }
- wait:
    frames: 12
- create:
    box: learned_material
    name: editable learned material
    frame:
      x: 400.0
      y: 340.0
      w: 420.0
      h: 100.0
    properties:
      code: |-
        import afield.graphics.shader.learning.LearnedShader

        // A separate scene: stop the original learned-shader box before launching this one.
        // Edit this box's fragment property while it runs; the network stays allocated.
        prop<AutoCloseable>(materialSession)
        fromContextWithNameOrNull<AutoCloseable>("materialSession")?.close()
        val owner = renderer
        val passName = "editable learned material"
        val learned = LearnedShader(owner, name = passName, attach = false)
        learned.view = 1
        learned.setParameter(.25f)
        prop<RenderToTexture>(learnedImage) = learned.output
        val material = moduleHere {
            depthTest = false
            depthWrite = false
            blend = false
        }
        val triangle = Mesh(owner, material)
        triangle.resize(3, 0, material)
        material += "fullscreen" to triangle

        // Compute and resolve run before this ordinary fragment shader samples their RTT.
        owner.renderList.preTargets[passName] = learned
        owner.renderList.modules[passName] = material
        var closed = false
        materialSession = AutoCloseable {
            if (!closed) {
                closed = true
                owner.renderList.modules.remove(passName, material)
                if (!owner.isClosed) {
                    learned.close()
                    owner.cleanup += Runnable { material.current.cleanup() }
                }
            }
        }
        val ownedSession = materialSession
        println(
            "Edit fragment: the learnedImage texture comes from the unchanged network. Stop the original comparison box to avoid rendering it too.",
        )
        frames { while (!closed && !owner.isClosed) frame() }.end { ownedSession.close() }
      vertex: "#version 460\nlayout(location=0) out vec2 uv;\nvoid main() {\n    vec2 p=vec2((gl_VertexIndex<<1)&2,gl_VertexIndex&2);\n\
        \    uv=vec2(p.x,1-p.y);\n    gl_Position=vec4(p*2-1,0,1);\n}\n"
      fragment: "#version 460\nlayout(set=0,binding=0) uniform sampler2D learnedImage;\nlayout(location=0) in vec2\
        \ uv;\nlayout(location=0) out vec4 color;\nvoid main() {\n    // The left half is the model's RGB; the right\
        \ is an editable treatment.\n    vec2 st=vec2(fract(uv.x*2),uv.y);\n    vec3 base=texture(learnedImage,st).rgb;\n\
        \    vec3 treatment=mix(base,base.gbr,.65);\n    treatment*=.85+.15*sin(st.y*160);\n    color=vec4(uv.x<.5\
        \ ? base : treatment,1);\n}\n"
- connect:
    parent: agent_graphics_context
    child: learned_material

before:
name: optical_flow
description: Hardware image motion, cost inspection and feedback advection from a pair of Field images.
operations:
- create:
    box: agent_graphics_context
    name: renderer
    frame:
      x: 40.0
      y: 40.0
      w: 300.0
      h: 100.0

- wait:
    frames: 3
- create:
    box: optical_flow
    name: optical flow
    frame:
      x: 400.0
      y: 160.0
      w: 420.0
      h: 100.0
    properties:
      code: |-
        import afield.media.vision.*

        prop<OpticalFlowDemo>(lab)
        fromContextWithNameOrNull<OpticalFlowDemo>("lab")?.close()
        // AUTO: the VK_NV_optical_flow engine where the device has one, portable pyramidal Lucas–Kanade everywhere else.
        lab = OpticalFlowDemo(renderer, backend = OpticalFlowBackend.AUTO)
        println("Optical flow backend: ${lab.flow.backend}")
        var gain = 1f
        var damping = .98f
        // The two backends report cost on different scales, so the rejection threshold starts at the demo's per-backend
        // default.
        var cost = lab.costThreshold
        var deform = true
        var reset = false
        controlGroup("optical flow") {
            slider("Advection gain", min = 0.0, max = 3.0, initialValue = 1.0) { gain = it.toFloat() }
            slider("Feedback retention", min = 0.0, max = .995, initialValue = .98) { damping = it.toFloat() }
            slider(
                "Reject cost above",
                min = 0.0,
                max = 6.0 * lab.costDisplayRange,
                initialValue = lab.costThreshold.toDouble(),
            ) {
                cost = it.toFloat()
            }
            checkbox("Consecutive-frame wiggle", initialValue = true) {
                deform = it
                reset = true
            }
            button("Reset feedback and motion hints") { if (it) reset = true }
        }
        displayOpen("optical flow")
        println(
            "Top: consecutive frames. Below: motion/cost and advected feedback. Turn off wiggle for the (+12, -8) translation check.",
        )
        frames {
            var time = 0f
            while (true) {
                lab.dx = if (deform) 0f else 12f
                lab.dy = if (deform) 0f else -8f
                lab.displayRange = if (deform) 3f else 20f
                lab.gain = gain
                lab.damping = damping
                lab.costThreshold = cost
                lab.deformation = deform
                lab.update(time, reset)
                reset = false
                time += lab.pairStep
                frame()
            }
        }
            .end { lab.close() }

    parent: agent_graphics_context
    child: optical_flow

          "Top: consecutive frames. Below: motion/cost and advected feedback. Turn off wiggle for the (+12, -8) translation check.",
      )
      frames {

before:
# Neural reconstruction

**Keep the same output size, and change how Field gets there.** DLAA reconstructs the native-resolution
image to smooth edges. DLSS Super Resolution starts with a smaller render and reconstructs it to the
same output size. Both run inside Field's Vulkan renderer; neither needs ray tracing.

The [neural_reconstruction](agent_transcripts.md#neural_reconstruction) Starting Point compares the original image, DLAA, Quality and Performance
at **1920 × 1080**, with Ultra Performance for pushing the source down to 360p.
Its crossing rods, checkerboard surfaces and moving highlights make the differences
easy to see. Switch to **Abstract colors and particles** to try less conventional imagery.

![Thin crossing geometry reconstructed with DLAA](assets/neural_reconstruction/dlaa.png)

## Open the experiment

On Field's welcome screen, search **Starting points** for **neural_reconstruction** and open an editable
copy. Run the **renderer** box, then **neural reconstruction**. The controls appear in that box; the image
appears in the native graphics window.

- **0: Source** shows the unjittered native-resolution scene.
- **1: DLAA** applies neural antialiasing at native resolution.
- **2: Quality** renders at the SDK's recommended size and reconstructs to 1080p.
- **3: Performance** uses a smaller input, again producing 1080p.
- **4: Ultra** selects Ultra Performance: **640 × 360 → 1920 × 1080** on this machine,
  nine output pixels for each source pixel.
- **Animate** and **Move camera** let you separate changing shading from camera motion.
- **Camera cut / reset** jumps the scene forward and discards temporal history.

The mode control replaces the reconstruction context at a frame boundary. You can return to Source
immediately. If NGX is unavailable, the scene opens in Source mode and prints the reason. Minimizing
Field's window and restoring it keeps the loop responsive and resumes DLAA output where it left off.

![The reconstruction box's controls: the mode slider set to 4 of Source/DLAA/Quality/Performance/Ultra, an unchecked Abstract colors and particles box, Animate and Move camera both checked, and hold-to-press Camera cut / reset and Reload edited shaders buttons](assets/neural_reconstruction/controls.png)

## Comparing the modes in motion

The following comparisons show consecutive rendered frames at 30 frames per second. Each includes a
deliberate camera cut halfway through. All four modes use the same scene times and output size.

<video controls muted loop playsinline preload="metadata" src="assets/neural_reconstruction/geometry.mp4" poster="../assets/neural_reconstruction/dlaa-geometry.png" width="3840" height="2160" style="max-width:100%;height:auto;aspect-ratio:16/9"></video>

Top left: Source. Top right: DLAA. Bottom left: Quality. Bottom right: Performance. Open the video
fullscreen to inspect the thin edges.

Neural reconstruction uses earlier frames. Geometric motion can describe a moving particle or camera,
but cannot describe every changing fragment function. The abstract scene deliberately changes colors
without moving their surfaces, so it is also a way to inspect the limits of reconstruction.

<video controls muted loop playsinline preload="metadata" src="assets/neural_reconstruction/abstract.mp4" poster="../assets/neural_reconstruction/dlaa-abstract.png" width="3840" height="2160" style="max-width:100%;height:auto;aspect-ratio:16/9"></video>

For imagery whose abrupt changes should remain abrupt, use Source or draw that layer after
reconstruction. This example is opaque RGB only: it does not handle alpha coverage, translucent
compositing or latent pigment channels. The adapter does not invent a velocity for changing colors.

## Push the source smaller

Keep the output at 1080p and move the mode control to **4: Ultra**. Its **640 × 360** source has
only **11.1% of the output pixels**, and 44.4% as many pixels as Performance's 960 × 540 input.
The pinned SDK reports 640 × 360 as both the minimum and maximum for Ultra at this output size;
320 × 180 is outside its supported range. The box prints the runtime limit.

Switching creates a fresh context and resets history, so previous higher-resolution frames cannot
carry the smaller source through the comparison.

<video controls muted loop playsinline preload="metadata" src="assets/neural_reconstruction/stress-geometry.mp4" poster="../assets/neural_reconstruction/stress-ultra_performance-geometry.png" width="3840" height="2160" style="max-width:100%;height:auto;aspect-ratio:16/9"></video>

Top left: native Source. Top right: Performance. Bottom left: Ultra. Bottom right: Ultra's own
360p input enlarged with **nearest-neighbour scaling**, without reconstruction. Each panel fills
1920 × 1080; its label gives the source dimensions. Watch the crossing
rods and checkerboards, especially after the cut halfway through.

<video controls muted loop playsinline preload="metadata" src="assets/neural_reconstruction/stress-abstract.mp4" poster="../assets/neural_reconstruction/stress-ultra_performance-abstract.png" width="3840" height="2160" style="max-width:100%;height:auto;aspect-ratio:16/9"></video>

The abstract version stresses changing color and small particles as well as geometry. Stop **Animate**
and **Move camera** to inspect how much improves with history, then use **Camera cut / reset** to
discard it. The [smaller-input measurements](assets/neural_reconstruction/stress-measurements.json)
record the actual size limits, motion check and GPU timings.

## Change it while it runs

Edit the **vertex** or **fragment** property of the scene box, then press **Reload edited shaders**.
A compilation error keeps the last working image. A change to inputs, outputs or resource layout is
rejected; create a new scene for that change. A successful compatible edit resets reconstruction history.

The reusable scene is also a small piece of ordinary Field code:

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
import afield.media.reconstruction.*

val experiment = ReconstructionDemo(
    renderer,
    ReconstructionMode.DLAA,
    ReconstructionSize(1920, 1080),
)
experiment.abstractScene = true
experiment.reset("material edit")

// experiment.close() when replacing it
```

`renderer` comes from the parent renderer box. `mode = null` selects Source. The example contains the
controls and shader properties needed to keep editing, rather than requiring a separate launch script.

For Ultra Performance in your own experiment:

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val outputSize = ReconstructionSize(1920, 1080)
val mode = ReconstructionMode.ULTRA_PERFORMANCE
val experiment = ReconstructionDemo(renderer, mode, outputSize)
```

You can also pass an explicit `inputSize` between the reported minimum and maximum. Unsupported
dimensions are rejected before scene images are allocated. DLAA still requires native resolution.

For your own image pipeline, query `DlssReconstruction.recommend(renderer, outputSize, mode)` first.
Create render targets at the returned input size, render with `ReconstructionJitter.halton(...)`, then
call `evaluate(command, ReconstructionInputs(color, depth, motion), frame)` after the producer has
finished its render pass. Present `output` or use it in another Field pass. Keep the source for bypass.

Each input must follow these conventions:

| Input | Convention |
|---|---|
| Color | Opaque linear HDR RGB, explicit pre-exposure; UI added afterward |
| Depth | Vulkan 0–1, ordinary Z, background 1 |
| Motion | Current pixel → previous pixel, input-pixel units, X right/Y down, no jitter |
| Jitter | Projection displacement in input pixels, matching the rendered image |
| Reset | Camera cuts, live edits, new resources, skipped frames and context recreation |

For Field's direct-lighting motion texture, declare its current-minus-previous UV convention:

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
ReconstructionInputs(
    color,
    depth,
    motion,
    motionCurrentMinusPrevious = true,
    motionInPixels = false,
)
```

The adapter supplies the sign and input dimensions to NGX for both Super Resolution and Ray
Reconstruction. The motion texture stays on the GPU and needs no conversion pass.

??? aside "Inspect the input guides"

    This depth image uses logarithmic display scaling to make its structure visible:

    ![The scene depth, displayed with logarithmic scaling](assets/neural_reconstruction/depth.png)

    In the known-translation check, the whole scene moves four input pixels right. Its motion guide
    must point four pixels left. The colored foreground below encodes X/Y velocity; the maximum
    measured error was below 0.001 pixel. The background is a constant field with zero motion.

    ![Current-to-previous motion for the four-pixel translation](assets/neural_reconstruction/motion.png)

## On the RTX 4090

On this Linux machine (RTX 4090, driver 610.43.02), 100 measurements after warm-up gave:

| Mode | Render → output | NGX median / 95th percentile |
|---|---|---|
| DLAA | 1920 × 1080 → 1920 × 1080 | 5.44 / 5.52 ms |
| Quality | 1280 × 720 → 1920 × 1080 | 4.92 / 5.01 ms |
| Performance | 960 × 540 → 1920 × 1080 | 6.23 / 6.30 ms |
| Ultra Performance | 640 × 360 → 1920 × 1080 | 5.25 / 5.29 ms |

Read that table across rather than down: Ultra takes one ninth of the output pixel count as input
and does **not** cost a ninth as much to reconstruct. A mode named Performance does not promise a
cheaper reconstruction pass either — the saving is in rendering the smaller source, which is yours.

On the crossing rods, against an independently rendered four-sample reference, static linear-RGB mean
squared error fell from **0.000233** for Source to **0.0000708** for DLAA, a **69.6% reduction**.
That is a number about thin edges in this scene, and abstract imagery behaves differently.

Each 1080p reconstruction output allocation is 16.9 MiB on this driver. The SDK reported 89.7, 172.4
and 206.0 MiB of device allocations as DLAA, Quality and Performance were created in sequence; these figures include
its retained device cache and must not be added together as independent per-view costs.

Every timing above is the NGX evaluation and its surrounding barriers, so add your own scene render
to it to get a frame. The [measurement report](assets/neural_reconstruction/measurements.json)
includes the device capability report, sample counts, memory and motion-vector errors; Ultra's row
comes from the separate smaller-input run.

## Optional installation

This experiment uses native Linux Vulkan NGX, with NVIDIA's public DLSS SDK pinned to
[`3749594`](https://github.com/NVIDIA/DLSS/tree/374959484e79a640feaba44c93ac8cfb0a03f5b5), library version
310.9.1. The SDK is separately licensed; Field does not bundle its binaries. Ordinary builds and the
Source view work without it.

??? aside "Build the optional adapter in a source checkout"

    Obtain that revision of NVIDIA/DLSS, then build Field's small wrapper:

    ```diffstatic {data-lang=bash}
    FIELD_DLSS_ROOT=/path/to/DLSS bash tools/lighting/build_ngx.sh
    ```

    Launch Field with the same `FIELD_DLSS_ROOT`. The wrapper defaults to
    `build/native/field-ngx/libfield_ngx.so`; `FIELD_NGX_LIBRARY` can select another location.

    `FIELD_NGX_DISABLE=1` disables the adapter for fallback testing.

# Neural reconstruction

**Keep the same output size, and change how Field gets there.** DLAA reconstructs the native-resolution
image to smooth edges. DLSS Super Resolution starts with a smaller render and reconstructs it to the
same output size. Both run inside Field's Vulkan renderer; neither needs ray tracing.

The [neural_reconstruction](agent_transcripts.md#neural_reconstruction) Starting Point compares the original image, DLAA, Quality and Performance
at **1920 × 1080**, with Ultra Performance for pushing the source down to 360p.
Its crossing rods, checkerboard surfaces and moving highlights make the differences
easy to see. Switch to **Abstract colors and particles** to try less conventional imagery.

![Thin crossing geometry reconstructed with DLAA](assets/neural_reconstruction/dlaa.png)

## Open the experiment

On Field's welcome screen, search **Starting points** for **neural_reconstruction** and open an editable
copy. Run the **renderer** box, then **neural reconstruction**. The controls appear in that box; the image
appears in the native graphics window.

- **0: Source** shows the unjittered native-resolution scene.
- **1: DLAA** applies neural antialiasing at native resolution.
- **2: Quality** renders at the SDK's recommended size and reconstructs to 1080p.
- **3: Performance** uses a smaller input, again producing 1080p.
- **4: Ultra** selects Ultra Performance: **640 × 360 → 1920 × 1080** on this machine,
  nine output pixels for each source pixel.
- **Animate** and **Move camera** let you separate changing shading from camera motion.
- **Camera cut / reset** jumps the scene forward and discards temporal history.

The mode control replaces the reconstruction context at a frame boundary. You can return to Source
immediately. If NGX is unavailable, the scene opens in Source mode and prints the reason. Minimizing
Field's window and restoring it keeps the loop responsive and resumes DLAA output where it left off.

![The reconstruction box's controls: the mode slider set to 4 of Source/DLAA/Quality/Performance/Ultra, an unchecked Abstract colors and particles box, Animate and Move camera both checked, and hold-to-press Camera cut / reset and Reload edited shaders buttons](assets/neural_reconstruction/controls.png)

## Comparing the modes in motion

The following comparisons show consecutive rendered frames at 30 frames per second. Each includes a
deliberate camera cut halfway through. All four modes use the same scene times and output size.

<video controls muted loop playsinline preload="metadata" src="assets/neural_reconstruction/geometry.mp4" poster="../assets/neural_reconstruction/dlaa-geometry.png" width="3840" height="2160" style="max-width:100%;height:auto;aspect-ratio:16/9"></video>

Top left: Source. Top right: DLAA. Bottom left: Quality. Bottom right: Performance. Open the video
fullscreen to inspect the thin edges.

Neural reconstruction uses earlier frames. Geometric motion can describe a moving particle or camera,
but cannot describe every changing fragment function. The abstract scene deliberately changes colors
without moving their surfaces, so it is also a way to inspect the limits of reconstruction.

<video controls muted loop playsinline preload="metadata" src="assets/neural_reconstruction/abstract.mp4" poster="../assets/neural_reconstruction/dlaa-abstract.png" width="3840" height="2160" style="max-width:100%;height:auto;aspect-ratio:16/9"></video>

For imagery whose abrupt changes should remain abrupt, use Source or draw that layer after
reconstruction. This example is opaque RGB only: it does not handle alpha coverage, translucent
compositing or latent pigment channels. The adapter does not invent a velocity for changing colors.

## Push the source smaller

Keep the output at 1080p and move the mode control to **4: Ultra**. Its **640 × 360** source has
only **11.1% of the output pixels**, and 44.4% as many pixels as Performance's 960 × 540 input.
The pinned SDK reports 640 × 360 as both the minimum and maximum for Ultra at this output size;
320 × 180 is outside its supported range. The box prints the runtime limit.

Switching creates a fresh context and resets history, so previous higher-resolution frames cannot
carry the smaller source through the comparison.

<video controls muted loop playsinline preload="metadata" src="assets/neural_reconstruction/stress-geometry.mp4" poster="../assets/neural_reconstruction/stress-ultra_performance-geometry.png" width="3840" height="2160" style="max-width:100%;height:auto;aspect-ratio:16/9"></video>

Top left: native Source. Top right: Performance. Bottom left: Ultra. Bottom right: Ultra's own
360p input enlarged with **nearest-neighbour scaling**, without reconstruction. Each panel fills
1920 × 1080; its label gives the source dimensions. Watch the crossing
rods and checkerboards, especially after the cut halfway through.

<video controls muted loop playsinline preload="metadata" src="assets/neural_reconstruction/stress-abstract.mp4" poster="../assets/neural_reconstruction/stress-ultra_performance-abstract.png" width="3840" height="2160" style="max-width:100%;height:auto;aspect-ratio:16/9"></video>

The abstract version stresses changing color and small particles as well as geometry. Stop **Animate**
and **Move camera** to inspect how much improves with history, then use **Camera cut / reset** to
discard it. The [smaller-input measurements](assets/neural_reconstruction/stress-measurements.json)
record the actual size limits, motion check and GPU timings.

## Change it while it runs

Edit the **vertex** or **fragment** property of the scene box, then press **Reload edited shaders**.
A compilation error keeps the last working image. A change to inputs, outputs or resource layout is
rejected; create a new scene for that change. A successful compatible edit resets reconstruction history.

The reusable scene is also a small piece of ordinary Field code:

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
import afield.media.reconstruction.*

val experiment = ReconstructionDemo(
    renderer,
    ReconstructionMode.DLAA,
    ReconstructionSize(1920, 1080),
)
experiment.abstractScene = true
experiment.reset("material edit")

// The constructing box run owns this view; Stop or rerun closes it.
```

`ReconstructionDemo` registers with the constructing box run immediately. Stop or rerun
detaches its exact view and releases its resources. `renderer` comes from the parent renderer box. `mode = null` selects Source. The example contains the
controls and shader properties needed to keep editing, rather than requiring a separate launch script.

For Ultra Performance in your own experiment:

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val outputSize = ReconstructionSize(1920, 1080)
val mode = ReconstructionMode.ULTRA_PERFORMANCE
val experiment = ReconstructionDemo(renderer, mode, outputSize)
```

You can also pass an explicit `inputSize` between the reported minimum and maximum. Unsupported
dimensions are rejected before scene images are allocated. DLAA still requires native resolution.

For your own image pipeline, query `DlssReconstruction.recommend(renderer, outputSize, mode)` first.
Create render targets at the returned input size, render with `ReconstructionJitter.halton(...)`, then
call `evaluate(command, ReconstructionInputs(color, depth, motion), frame)` after the producer has
finished its render pass. Present `output` or use it in another Field pass. Keep the source for bypass.

Each input must follow these conventions:

| Input | Convention |
|---|---|
| Color | Opaque linear HDR RGB, explicit pre-exposure; UI added afterward |
| Depth | Vulkan 0–1, ordinary Z, background 1 |
| Motion | Current pixel → previous pixel, input-pixel units, X right/Y down, no jitter |
| Jitter | Projection displacement in input pixels, matching the rendered image |
| Reset | Camera cuts, live edits, new resources, skipped frames and context recreation |

For Field's direct-lighting motion texture, declare its current-minus-previous UV convention:

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
ReconstructionInputs(
    color,
    depth,
    motion,
    motionCurrentMinusPrevious = true,
    motionInPixels = false,
)
```

The adapter supplies the sign and input dimensions to NGX for both Super Resolution and Ray
Reconstruction. The motion texture stays on the GPU and needs no conversion pass.

??? aside "Inspect the input guides"

    This depth image uses logarithmic display scaling to make its structure visible:

    ![The scene depth, displayed with logarithmic scaling](assets/neural_reconstruction/depth.png)

    In the known-translation check, the whole scene moves four input pixels right. Its motion guide
    must point four pixels left. The colored foreground below encodes X/Y velocity; the maximum
    measured error was below 0.001 pixel. The background is a constant field with zero motion.

    ![Current-to-previous motion for the four-pixel translation](assets/neural_reconstruction/motion.png)

## On the RTX 4090

On this Linux machine (RTX 4090, driver 610.43.02), 100 measurements after warm-up gave:

| Mode | Render → output | NGX median / 95th percentile |
|---|---|---|
| DLAA | 1920 × 1080 → 1920 × 1080 | 5.44 / 5.52 ms |
| Quality | 1280 × 720 → 1920 × 1080 | 4.92 / 5.01 ms |
| Performance | 960 × 540 → 1920 × 1080 | 6.23 / 6.30 ms |
| Ultra Performance | 640 × 360 → 1920 × 1080 | 5.25 / 5.29 ms |

Read that table across rather than down: Ultra takes one ninth of the output pixel count as input
and does **not** cost a ninth as much to reconstruct. A mode named Performance does not promise a
cheaper reconstruction pass either — the saving is in rendering the smaller source, which is yours.

On the crossing rods, against an independently rendered four-sample reference, static linear-RGB mean
squared error fell from **0.000233** for Source to **0.0000708** for DLAA, a **69.6% reduction**.
That is a number about thin edges in this scene, and abstract imagery behaves differently.

Each 1080p reconstruction output allocation is 16.9 MiB on this driver. The SDK reported 89.7, 172.4
and 206.0 MiB of device allocations as DLAA, Quality and Performance were created in sequence; these figures include
its retained device cache and must not be added together as independent per-view costs.

Every timing above is the NGX evaluation and its surrounding barriers, so add your own scene render
to it to get a frame. The [measurement report](assets/neural_reconstruction/measurements.json)
includes the device capability report, sample counts, memory and motion-vector errors; Ultra's row
comes from the separate smaller-input run.
